value.statement: All J_i for i∈I are the same nonzero finitely generated R-submodule J⊂ℂ. Under ι_M, M_R=⊕_(i∈I) J e_i: the map γ↦Σ_(i∈I)γ(i)e_i is an R-linear bijection J^I→M_R. The multiplication map μ:ℚ⊗_R J→ℂ, μ(q⊗c)=qc, is injective with image the rational span of J, and dim_ℚ(ℚ⊗_R J)=1. There exists b∈J with b≠0 and J=Rb; for every such b the vectors (b e_i)_(i∈I) form an R-basis of M_R.

value.statement: The integer map extends to a ring map R→K. For every pair of integers A₀,B₀ with B₀≠0 and p∤B₀ it sends A₀/B₀ to (A₀·1_K)(B₀·1_K)^(-1). Also R/pR≅F_p via the residue of A₀/B₀↦[A₀][B₀]^(-1). There are K-linear isomorphisms Γ:V_K→M_R⊗_R K and Δ:M_R⊗_R K→(M_R/pM_R)⊗_(F_p)K. They satisfy Γ(m⊗c)=(1⊗m)⊗c, Γ^(-1)((r⊗m)⊗c)=m⊗(r̄c), Δ(z⊗c)=[z]⊗c, and Δ^(-1)([z]⊗c)=z⊗c, where r̄ denotes the image of r in K. They intertwine induced lattice operators. There exist b∈J\{0} with J=Rb and a family β:I→V_K such that β_i=Γ^(-1)((b e_i)⊗1) for i∈I and β is a K-basis of V_K; here b e_i is regarded as the unique element of M_R mapping to that vector by ι_M. In particular dim_K(V_K)=n>0. Write a=ρ_K(x⊗1), d=ρ_K(y⊗1), t=ρ_K(h⊗1). On this basis aβ_0=0, aβ_i=(λ−i+1)β_(i−1) for i≥1; dβ_i=(i+1)β_(i+1) for i<λ and dβ_λ=0; tβ_i=(λ−2i)β_i. All integers in these formulas are mapped into K. For every integer s with 0≤s≤λ, s!≠0 in K and the lattice-induced X(s),Y(s) on V_K equal (s!)^(-1)a^s and (s!)^(-1)d^s. For i,j∈I let T_ij=binom(λ,j)^(-1)((λ−i)!)^(-1)a^(λ−i) (λ!)^(-1)d^λ (λ!)^(-1)a^λ ((λ−j)!)^(-1)d^(λ−j), with rightmost operator applied first and all scalar factors in K. Then binom(λ,j)≠0 in K and T_ij β_k=β_i when k=j and zero when k≠j. Thus T_ij are the coordinate matrix units for this K-basis.

value.N001: n=λ+1>0 and |I|=n. The vectors (e_i)_(i∈I) form a complex basis of V. For every integer t≥0, h y^t v=(λ−2t)y^t v, and for t≥1, x y^t v=t(λ−t+1)y^(t−1)v. Moreover y^(λ+1)v=0 and all higher powers on v vanish. Their action matrices are x e_0=0, x e_i=(λ−i+1)e_(i−1) for 1≤i≤λ; y e_i=(i+1)e_(i+1) for 0≤i<λ, y e_λ=0; h e_i=(λ−2i)e_i for i∈I. For every integer r≥0 and i∈I, X(r)e_i=binom(λ−i+r,r)e_(i−r) if r≤i and zero otherwise; Y(r)e_i=binom(i+r,r)e_(i+r) if i+r≤λ and zero otherwise. Each displayed nonzero coefficient is an integer. Here binom(a,r)=a!/(r!(a−r)!) for integers 0≤r≤a; these are the usual integer binomial coefficients.
value.N002: R is the subring ℤ_(p) of ℚ⊂ℂ. The map ι_M:R⊗_ℤ M→V is injective. With M_R identified with its image it is a free R-module with an R-basis of n elements and its complex span is V. Each X(r),Y(r), r≥0, preserves M and M_R. The operators x,y,h preserve M; ℤx+ℤy+ℤh is closed under the Lie bracket. For t∈ℤx+ℤy+ℤh, m∈M and c,d∈K, the rule (t⊗c)(m⊗d)=tm⊗(cd) is well-defined on (ℤx+ℤy+ℤh)⊗_ℤ K and V_K=M⊗_ℤ K and defines a K-linear Lie action. For every integer 0≤r≤λ, p∤r!, so r! is a unit in R. For all i,j∈I, binom(λ,j) is a unit in R and Π=E_λλ, X(λ−i)Π=E_iλ, ΠY(λ−j)=binom(λ,j)E_λj, and E_ij=binom(λ,j)^(-1)X(λ−i)ΠY(λ−j). Consequently all E_ij preserve M_R.
value.N003: All J_i for i∈I are the same nonzero finitely generated R-submodule J⊂ℂ. Under ι_M, M_R=⊕_(i∈I) J e_i: the map γ↦Σ_(i∈I)γ(i)e_i is an R-linear bijection J^I→M_R. The multiplication map μ:ℚ⊗_R J→ℂ, μ(q⊗c)=qc, is injective with image the rational span of J, and dim_ℚ(ℚ⊗_R J)=1. There exists b∈J with b≠0 and J=Rb; for every such b the vectors (b e_i)_(i∈I) form an R-basis of M_R.
value.N004: The integer map extends to a ring map R→K. For every pair of integers A₀,B₀ with B₀≠0 and p∤B₀ it sends A₀/B₀ to (A₀·1_K)(B₀·1_K)^(-1). Also R/pR≅F_p via the residue of A₀/B₀↦[A₀][B₀]^(-1). There are K-linear isomorphisms Γ:V_K→M_R⊗_R K and Δ:M_R⊗_R K→(M_R/pM_R)⊗_(F_p)K. They satisfy Γ(m⊗c)=(1⊗m)⊗c, Γ^(-1)((r⊗m)⊗c)=m⊗(r̄c), Δ(z⊗c)=[z]⊗c, and Δ^(-1)([z]⊗c)=z⊗c, where r̄ denotes the image of r in K. They intertwine induced lattice operators. There exist b∈J\{0} with J=Rb and a family β:I→V_K such that β_i=Γ^(-1)((b e_i)⊗1) for i∈I and β is a K-basis of V_K; here b e_i is regarded as the unique element of M_R mapping to that vector by ι_M. In particular dim_K(V_K)=n>0. Write a=ρ_K(x⊗1), d=ρ_K(y⊗1), t=ρ_K(h⊗1). On this basis aβ_0=0, aβ_i=(λ−i+1)β_(i−1) for i≥1; dβ_i=(i+1)β_(i+1) for i<λ and dβ_λ=0; tβ_i=(λ−2i)β_i. All integers in these formulas are mapped into K. For every integer s with 0≤s≤λ, s!≠0 in K and the lattice-induced X(s),Y(s) on V_K equal (s!)^(-1)a^s and (s!)^(-1)d^s. For i,j∈I let T_ij=binom(λ,j)^(-1)((λ−i)!)^(-1)a^(λ−i) (λ!)^(-1)d^λ (λ!)^(-1)a^λ ((λ−j)!)^(-1)d^(λ−j), with rightmost operator applied first and all scalar factors in K. Then binom(λ,j)≠0 in K and T_ij β_k=β_i when k=j and zero when k≠j. Thus T_ij are the coordinate matrix units for this K-basis.
value.P: V_K is nonzero, and for every K-linear subspace W⊂V_K invariant under ρ_K(x⊗1), ρ_K(y⊗1), and ρ_K(h⊗1), either W={0} or W=V_K. Thus V(K) is irreducible as an L(K)-module, for every field K and every prime p and integer 0≤λ<p, including λ=0 and p=2.

value.text: H001 gives λ≥0, so n=λ+1>0 and I consists of exactly n integers. We prove the string identities simultaneously by natural induction on t≥0. At t=0, hv=λv and xv=0 are H003. In the induction step temporarily assume L1: h y^t v=(λ−2t)y^t v and, when t≥1, x y^t v=t(λ−t+1)y^(t−1)v (with xv=0 at t=0). The relation hy=yh−2y from H002 gives h y^(t+1)v=(λ−2t−2)y^(t+1)v. The relation xy=yx+h gives x y^(t+1)v=y(x y^t v)+h y^t v=[t(λ−t+1)+λ−2t]y^t v=(t+1)(λ−t)y^t v, also at t=0 using xv=0. This proves the step and discharges L1; natural induction gives both identities for all t in their stated ranges.

For each i∈I, repeated application of the x identity in F001 gives x^i y^i v=i!λ(λ−1)⋯(λ−i+1)v. At i=0 the product is empty and equals 1; at i≥1 its factors are positive integers, since i≤λ. Since v≠0 by H003, this shows e_i≠0 over ℂ. F001 gives h e_i=(λ−2i)e_i. To prove independence, fix coefficients c and temporarily assume L2: Σ_(i∈I)c_i e_i=0. Fix j∈I and apply ∏_(k∈I,k≠j)(h−(λ−2k)Id_V). Every term except j is zero; the j term is c_j [∏_(k≠j)2(k−j)]e_j. All its factors are nonzero complex numbers and e_j≠0, so c_j=0. Since j was arbitrary, all coefficients vanish. Discharging L2 proves independence.

Apply M001 to the division ring ℂ, the complex vector space V, the finite index set I and the family e. F002 supplies independence, F001 gives |I|=n, and H002 gives dim_ℂ V=λ+1=n and finite dimensionality. Thus the span of e is V, so together with independence it is a basis. By F001, y^(λ+1)v has eigenvalue −λ−2 under h. Expand this vector in the basis e; comparison of each coefficient in h y^(λ+1)v=(−λ−2)y^(λ+1)v gives [λ−2i−(−λ−2)] times that coefficient zero. For i∈I this multiplier is 2(λ+1−i)≠0 in ℂ. Every coefficient is zero, hence y^(λ+1)v=0. Applying further powers of y gives all higher vanishing.

For arbitrary i∈I divide the identities F001 by i!: x e_0=0, and for i≥1, x e_i=(λ−i+1)e_(i−1). Directly y e_i=(i+1)e_(i+1) for i<λ, while y e_λ=0 by F003. Also h e_i=(λ−2i)e_i. These are the required integer action matrices.

Fix r≥0. Iterating the x matrix in F004 and dividing by r! gives X(r)e_i=[(λ−i+1)⋯(λ−i+r)/r!]e_(i−r)=binom(λ−i+r,r)e_(i−r) when r≤i. When r>i, iteration reaches x e_0=0 and gives zero. Similarly iteration of y gives Y(r)e_i=[(i+1)⋯(i+r)/r!]e_(i+r)=binom(i+r,r)e_(i+r) if i+r≤λ, and gives zero past the terminating string. These binomial coefficients have nonnegative top at least r. They are integers: for every nonnegative integer a₀, the factorial expressions have boundary values binom(a₀,0)=binom(a₀,a₀)=1 and satisfy binom(a₀,s)=binom(a₀−1,s−1)+binom(a₀−1,s) for 0<s<a₀ by a common-denominator calculation. Induction on a₀, proving the assertion simultaneously for all 0≤s≤a₀, proves integrality. This establishes every divided-power formula in the exported conclusion as well as its zero cases.

Since p is prime by H001, p≥2 and the integers not divisible by p are multiplicatively closed. Fraction addition and multiplication therefore make R a subring of ℚ⊂ℂ; in particular every integer b with p∤b is a unit, with inverse 1/b∈R. By H004 choose a simultaneous integer basis B of M and complex basis B of V. It has finitely many vectors since V has finite dimension n by H002. M010 applied to the nontrivial commutative ring ℂ supplies its strong rank condition. M003 applied to its complex basis gives that its number of vectors is dim_ℂ V=n. By N001, |I|=n; reindexing the basis by I yields the existence stated in F001.

Choose m as in F001. Apply M002 with R₀=ℤ, A=M, S₀=R and the integer basis m. It gives the R-basis (1⊗m_i)_(i∈I) of M_R. The map ι_M sends these basis vectors to m_i; a finite R-linear relation among their images is also a complex-linear relation, so all coefficients are zero. Thus ι_M is injective, identifies M_R with the R-span of the m_i inside V, and its complex span is V. For any r≥0, admissibility H004 and D005 imply X(r)M⊂M and Y(r)M⊂M; R-linearity gives preservation of M_R. In particular X(1)=x and Y(1)=y preserve M; H002 gives h=xy−yx on V, so h preserves M as well. The commutators in H002 show directly that the integer span of x,y,h is bracket-closed, since all three structure constants are integers. For arbitrary t₀∈ℤx+ℤy+ℤh and z_M∈M the restriction t₀z_M is in M. The rule (t₀⊗c₀)(z_M⊗d₀)=t₀z_M⊗(c₀d₀), for arbitrary c₀,d₀∈K, respects addition and both integer balancing relations, hence defines a K-bilinear action on the two tensor products. Its Lie representation identity is verified on pure tensors by the identity in the given complex Lie module V, and then on finite sums by bilinearity. Thus it is the asserted induced Lie action, without identifying the Chevalley integer form with any different reduction.

For every integer 0≤r≤λ, apply M006 with ℓ=p and u=r. H001 supplies primality and r≤λ<p, so p∤r!. Thus r! is a unit of R. In particular λ!, j!, (λ−j)! are all units, for j∈I. Their ratio binom(λ,j)=λ!/[j!(λ−j)!] is a unit of R, with inverse j!(λ−j)!/λ!. The factorials are positive and therefore nonzero as rational numbers. These statements also cover r=0.

We now identify operators by their actions on the complex basis e from N001. In Y(λ)X(λ), every basis vector below e_λ is killed by X(λ); on e_λ, X(λ)e_λ=e_0 and Y(λ)e_0=e_λ. Hence Π=E_λλ. Next X(λ−i)e_λ=e_i, with coefficient binom(λ−λ+λ−i,λ−i)=1, giving X(λ−i)Π=E_iλ. For ΠY(λ−j), an input e_k with k<j is carried below e_λ and killed by Π; if k>j the lowering string terminates and gives zero; on e_j its coefficient is binom(λ,λ−j)=binom(λ,j) and its image is e_λ. Therefore ΠY(λ−j)=binom(λ,j)E_λj. All statements include λ=0, when every factor is the identity on the one-dimensional space.

Combining F004, or applying it to each e_k, gives X(λ−i)ΠY(λ−j)=binom(λ,j)E_ij. Invert the coefficient using F003 to get E_ij=binom(λ,j)^(-1)X(λ−i)ΠY(λ−j). Every factor on the right preserves M_R by F002 and R-linearity, hence every E_ij preserves M_R. With F002 and F003 this proves the entire exported conclusion.

Use the embedding from N002 throughout to regard M_R as a submodule of V. By N001 its vectors have unique coordinates in e. Since E_ii preserves M_R by N002, the ith coordinate projection maps M_R onto J_i e_i. For arbitrary i,j₁∈I and c₁∈J_(j₁), E(i,j₁)(c₁ e_(j₁))=c₁ e_i∈M_R, giving J_(j₁)⊂J_i; the reverse inclusion follows by exchanging the two coordinate indices. Thus all J_i equal J. Choose the R-basis m of M_R supplied by N002. The finitely many ith coordinates of m generate J_i, since each vector of M_R is a finite R-linear combination of m, and conversely these coordinates lie in J_i by E_ii-stability. Hence J is finitely generated. It is nonzero: temporarily assume L1: J={0}. Then every coordinate projection of M_R would vanish, so M_R would be zero, contradicting its complex span V and the nonzero basis vector e_0 in N001. This contradiction discharges L1 and proves J≠{0}. Finally the maps M_R→J^I taking coordinates, and (c_i)↦Σ c_i e_i, are mutually inverse R-linear maps. The latter sum is in M_R since each c_i e_i is; independence in N001 gives uniqueness. This proves the direct sum decomposition without any rank assumption on a submodule of ℂ.

Define U and μ as declared, and choose a nonempty finite list g of nonzero R-generators of J from F001; let k≥1 be its length, and write it g_1,...,g_k. For any rational q₀ and any finite R-linear combination Σ_(j=1)^k r_j g_j, tensor bilinearity gives q₀⊗Σ r_j g_j=Σ(q₀r_j)(1⊗g_j). Consequently the finite set {1⊗g_j:1≤j≤k} spans U over ℚ. Apply M008 with F=ℚ and A=U to this finite set; since the span is all of U, U is finite-dimensional. To check injectivity of μ, let s₀≥0 be arbitrary, take arbitrary families Q_1,...,Q_(s₀)∈ℚ and C_1,...,C_(s₀)∈J, and set z₀=Σ_(l=1)^(s₀)Q_l⊗C_l. Every element of the algebraic tensor product has such a finite-sum presentation. Define D to be the product of the positive denominators of the Q_l (the empty product is 1), and put H_l=D Q_l∈ℤ. Then D is a nonzero integer and tensor balancing over R, which contains ℤ, gives z₀=(1/D)⊗Σ H_l C_l. Temporarily assume L2: μ(z₀)=0. Its image is (1/D)Σ H_l C_l, so Σ H_l C_l=0 in ℂ, hence z₀=0 in U. Discharge L2. Since the finite presentation was arbitrary, the kernel of μ is zero, which proves injectivity by applying this to the difference of any two tensors with equal images. Its image is exactly span_ℚ J, since it consists of finite rational combinations of elements of J and contains them all.

Define T=ℚ⊗_R M_R. The inclusion R⊂ℚ gives a commutative R-algebra structure on ℚ. Apply M002 to the R-basis m: the n vectors 1⊗m_i form a ℚ-basis of T. M010 applies to the nontrivial commutative ring ℚ. M003 with this basis gives dim_ℚ T=n, since |I|=n by N001.

Define Θ:T→U^I by Θ(q₀⊗Σ c_i e_i)=(q₀⊗c_i)_i, and define Ψ in the reverse direction by summing the maps q₀⊗c↦q₀⊗(c e_i) on coordinates. The coordinate maps in F001 are R-linear, so these balanced maps extend to ℚ-linear maps of the indicated tensor products. The composites ΘΨ and ΨΘ are identities: on an elementary tensor in a single coordinate the first is that same coordinate tensor, and on q₀⊗z the second is q₀⊗Σ c_i e_i=q₀⊗z. Additivity and generation by pure tensors prove the identities everywhere. Therefore Θ is a linear equivalence. Set r_J=dim_ℚ U. By F002, U is finitely generated over ℚ, and M009 says it is free. With M010 supplying the strong rank condition for ℚ, apply M004 to the finite constant family U indexed by I; it gives dim_ℚ(U^I)=Σ_(i∈I)r_J=n r_J. Apply M005 to Θ and combine with F003 to obtain n=n r_J. Since n>0 by N001, integer arithmetic yields r_J=1.

Choose a nonzero a∈J from F001. Then 1⊗a is nonzero in U, since μ(1⊗a)=a≠0. The singleton family consisting of 1⊗a is linearly independent: multiplying a putative scalar relation by μ gives that scalar times a zero in ℂ. Apply M001 over ℚ to this singleton and U, whose finite dimension is one by F002 and F004. It spans U. Consequently every 1⊗g_j is q_j(1⊗a) for some rational q_j; apply μ to get g_j=q_j a. As every g_j≠0, each q_j≠0. This proves existence of the full finite rational family needed next.

Choose q from F005, and fix 1≤j≤k. Write q_j=A/B with its nonzero integer numerator A and positive integer denominator B. By H001, p≥2, so p≠1. Apply M007 first to |A|≠0, then to B≠0, with ℓ=p. Choose d_N,u_N,d_D,u_D as in those applications, so |A|=p^d_N u_N, B=p^d_D u_D and neither u_N nor u_D is divisible by p. They are nonzero because A,B are. Hence q_j=p^(d_N−d_D)((A/|A|)u_N/u_D). Since A/|A| is either 1 or −1, the rational (A/|A|)u_N/u_D and its inverse belong to R by the defining denominator condition, so this factor is a unit. This proves, for every j in the finite list, the claimed decomposition into an integral power of p and a unit of R, and therefore the existence of simultaneous finite families in F006.

Choose ν_j,u_j from F006 and let ν be the minimum of the finite nonempty integer list ν_1,...,ν_k; choose j₀ attaining it. Such a minimum exists by repeatedly taking the smaller of two integers. Put b=p^ν a. This is nonzero, since p≠0 and a≠0. For each j, g_j=p^(ν_j−ν)u_j b lies in Rb because ν_j−ν≥0. Conversely g_(j₀)=u_(j₀)b, so b=u_(j₀)^(-1)g_(j₀) belongs to J. Thus the R-module generated by the g_j is exactly Rb, and J=Rb. Under F001, every vector of M_R is a sum Σ r_i b e_i, while any relation Σ r_i b e_i=0 has all r_i b=0 by the complex independence of e in N001, and hence all r_i=0. Thus (b e_i) is an R-basis. The same spanning and independence argument works for any nonzero b with J=Rb. Together with F001, F002 and F004 this proves the exported conclusion.

By H001, an integer maps to zero in K exactly when divisible by p. Thus for arbitrary integers A₀,B₀ with B₀≠0 and p∤B₀, the fraction A₀/B₀∈R has a nonzero denominator image in K; and φ(A₀/B₀)=(A₀·1_K)(B₀·1_K)^(-1) is defined. Equality of fractions follows by cross multiplication, so the formula is well-defined and preserves addition, multiplication and 1. The same formula in F_p gives ψ:R→F_p. It is onto, since every integer residue occurs, and its kernel is pR: ψ(A₀/B₀)=0 is equivalent to p∣A₀, hence A₀/B₀=p((A₀/p)/B₀). Conversely multiples of p have zero image. The induced map R/pR→F_p is therefore a bijective ring map. Both constructions agree with the usual inclusion F_p→K. Every unit of R has nonzero image in K, since its image has a multiplicative inverse. In particular N002 shows that r! for 0≤r≤λ and binom(λ,j), j∈I, have nonzero images in K.

Define Γ and Γ' by Γ(m⊗c)=(1⊗m)⊗c and Γ'((r⊗m)⊗c)=m⊗φ(r)c. The defining ℤ-balancing relations in R⊗_ℤ M and in M⊗_ℤ K, and the R-balancing relation in M_R⊗_R K, show that these formulas extend to K-linear maps. They are inverse: Γ'Γ(m⊗c)=m⊗c, and ΓΓ'((r⊗m)⊗c)=(1⊗m)⊗φ(r)c=(r⊗m)⊗c. These tensors generate, so the composites are identities. Next define Δ(z⊗c)=[z]⊗c and Δ'([z]⊗c)=z⊗c. Because p acts as zero on K, changing the lift z by pz' changes the second formula by pz'⊗c=z'⊗pc=0. Using F001, scalar balancing in F_p=R/pR gives the remaining balancing condition; thus both maps are well-defined and K-linear. Their composites are identities on pure tensors. This proves the two scalar-extension isomorphisms with exactly the formulas in the exported conclusion. An operator preserving M extends on all these tensors by applying it to the lattice factor; the displayed formulas commute with that operation. For Δ this also holds for any R-linear operator of M_R, since it preserves pM_R.

Choose b≠0 with J=Rb from N003. That input proves that (b e_i)_(i∈I), regarded in M_R via the injective map ι_M of N002, is an R-basis. Apply M002 with R₀=R, S₀=K and this basis, using φ from F001. It yields the K-basis (1⊗b e_i) of K⊗_R M_R. The tensor flip z⊗c↦c⊗z is K-linear, well-defined by balancing, and inverse to the reverse flip. Therefore (b e_i⊗1) is a basis of M_R⊗_R K. Transporting it by Γ^(-1) gives the K-basis β_i defined above: inverse linear maps carry spanning families to spanning families and relations to the same relations. Apply M010 to the nontrivial commutative field K, then M003 to β to obtain dim_K V_K=|I|=n>0 using N001.

Put a=ρ_K(x⊗1), d=ρ_K(y⊗1), t=ρ_K(h⊗1). By N001, complex linearity gives x(b e_i)=b x e_i, y(b e_i)=b y e_i, and h(b e_i)=b h e_i. N002 guarantees all these lattice operations are defined, and F002 transports their tensors. Thus aβ_0=0; aβ_i=(λ−i+1)β_(i−1) for i≥1; dβ_i=(i+1)β_(i+1) for i<λ, dβ_λ=0; tβ_i=(λ−2i)β_i. The coefficients are the images of the same integers in K. The identical reasoning using N001 for X(r),Y(r) gives their integral divided-power matrices on this basis for all r≥0, including the stated zero cases. Likewise each E_ij preserves M_R by N002 and acts there by E_ij(b e_k)=b e_i if k=j and equals zero otherwise, so its scalar extension, transported by Γ^(-1), is the coordinate matrix unit of β.

Fix 0≤r≤λ. As operators on M, the characteristic-zero definitions give r!X(r)=x^r and r!Y(r)=y^r; N002 gives their preservation of M. Tensoring these equalities gives the same equalities of induced operators on V_K. By F001, r!≠0 in K, so the induced divided powers equal (r!)^(-1)a^r and (r!)^(-1)d^r. The equality E_ij=binom(λ,j)^(-1)X(λ−i)Y(λ)X(λ)Y(λ−j) in N002 is an equality of R-linear operators on M_R. Extending scalars and transporting by Γ^(-1) preserves sums and compositions: this follows directly by evaluating on each pure tensor z⊗c. Substitute the divided-power equalities, whose indices λ−i, λ, λ−j all lie between 0 and λ. The result is T_ij=binom(λ,j)^(-1)((λ−i)!)^(-1)a^(λ−i) (λ!)^(-1)d^λ (λ!)^(-1)a^λ ((λ−j)!)^(-1)d^(λ−j), with rightmost factor applied first. Every scalar inverse exists by F001. F004 gives T_ij β_k=β_i if k=j and zero otherwise. Along with F001–F004 this proves every assertion of the exported conclusion, including the two natural tensor identifications and positive dimension.

N002 proves x,y,h preserve M and their integer span is a Lie algebra, which supplies the construction guard for ρ_K. Choose β from N004; set a,d,T as declared. N004 states that every scalar inverse in the polynomial T exists and T_ijβ_k equals β_i when k=j and zero otherwise. Fix any K-linear subspace W⊂V_K and temporarily assume L1: W is invariant under ρ_K(x⊗1), ρ_K(y⊗1), and ρ_K(h⊗1). Thus a and d preserve W. Repeated composition shows by finite induction that every nonnegative power of either preserves W; the identity also preserves W. Composing these powers and multiplying by K-scalars preserves W by the subspace axioms. Every polynomial T_ij in N004 therefore preserves W.

First temporarily assume L3: W={0}. Then the disjunction W={0} or W=V_K follows immediately; discharge L3, giving F002. For the other branch temporarily assume L2: W≠{0}. By this inequality and the subspace zero axiom, some nonzero vector lies in W. Expanding it in the basis β gives coefficients in K. If all coefficients were zero the vector would be zero, so at least one coefficient is nonzero. This establishes the simultaneous witnesses in F003 before choosing them.

Under L2 choose w,c,j from F003. For any i∈I, F001 and K-linearity give T_ij w=Σ_(k∈I)c_k T_ijβ_k=c_jβ_i∈W. Since c_j≠0 in the field K, multiplication by c_j^(-1) gives β_i∈W. As i was arbitrary, every vector in the basis β lies in W, so W=V_K. Discharge L2 to obtain F004.

The alternatives W={0} and W≠{0} exhaust all cases. F002 and F004 therefore yield W={0} or W=V_K. Discharge L1 and universally quantify the arbitrary W to obtain the required assertion for every invariant K-subspace. N001 gives n=λ+1>0 and N004 gives a K-basis of V_K of that cardinality, so V_K is nonzero. The three generators span L_K, so their invariant subspaces are exactly L_K-submodules by K-linearity of ρ_K. H001 includes λ=0 and p=2: at λ=0 all powers and factorials used in T are zeroth powers and 1; if p=2 then λ is 0 or 1, and all preceding invertibilities still hold. No distinctness of h-eigenvalues in K was used; distinctness was used only over ℂ in N001. K was used solely as a field of characteristic p, so it need not be algebraically closed. This proves the full exported target.

argument.text: Since p is prime by H001, p≥2 and the integers not divisible by p are multiplicatively closed. Fraction addition and multiplication therefore make R a subring of ℚ⊂ℂ; in particular every integer b with p∤b is a unit, with inverse 1/b∈R. By H004 choose a simultaneous integer basis B of M and complex basis B of V. It has finitely many vectors since V has finite dimension n by H002. M010 applied to the nontrivial commutative ring ℂ supplies its strong rank condition. M003 applied to its complex basis gives that its number of vectors is dim_ℂ V=n. By N001, |I|=n; reindexing the basis by I yields the existence stated in F001.

produces.statement: There exists a family m′:I→M which is a ℤ-basis of M and a complex basis of V.

argument.text: Choose m as in F001. Apply M002 with R₀=ℤ, A=M, S₀=R and the integer basis m. It gives the R-basis (1⊗m_i)_(i∈I) of M_R. The map ι_M sends these basis vectors to m_i; a finite R-linear relation among their images is also a complex-linear relation, so all coefficients are zero. Thus ι_M is injective, identifies M_R with the R-span of the m_i inside V, and its complex span is V. For any r≥0, admissibility H004 and D005 imply X(r)M⊂M and Y(r)M⊂M; R-linearity gives preservation of M_R. In particular X(1)=x and Y(1)=y preserve M; H002 gives h=xy−yx on V, so h preserves M as well. The commutators in H002 show directly that the integer span of x,y,h is bracket-closed, since all three structure constants are integers. For arbitrary t₀∈ℤx+ℤy+ℤh and z_M∈M the restriction t₀z_M is in M. The rule (t₀⊗c₀)(z_M⊗d₀)=t₀z_M⊗(c₀d₀), for arbitrary c₀,d₀∈K, respects addition and both integer balancing relations, hence defines a K-bilinear action on the two tensor products. Its Lie representation identity is verified on pure tensors by the identity in the given complex Lie module V, and then on finite sums by bilinearity. Thus it is the asserted induced Lie action, without identifying the Chevalley integer form with any different reduction.

produces.statement: ι_M is injective; the vectors 1⊗m_i form an R-basis of M_R of cardinality n and their images span V over ℂ. For every integer r′≥0, X(r′),Y(r′) preserve M and M_R. Also x,y,h preserve M, and ℤx+ℤy+ℤh is closed under brackets.

argument.text: For every integer 0≤r≤λ, apply M006 with ℓ=p and u=r. H001 supplies primality and r≤λ<p, so p∤r!. Thus r! is a unit of R. In particular λ!, j!, (λ−j)! are all units, for j∈I. Their ratio binom(λ,j)=λ!/[j!(λ−j)!] is a unit of R, with inverse j!(λ−j)!/λ!. The factorials are positive and therefore nonzero as rational numbers. These statements also cover r=0.

produces.statement: For all integers 0≤r′≤λ, p∤r′! and r′! is a unit in R. For every j′∈I, binom(λ,j′) is a unit of R, with inverse j′!(λ−j′)!/λ!.

argument.text: We now identify operators by their actions on the complex basis e from N001. In Y(λ)X(λ), every basis vector below e_λ is killed by X(λ); on e_λ, X(λ)e_λ=e_0 and Y(λ)e_0=e_λ. Hence Π=E_λλ. Next X(λ−i)e_λ=e_i, with coefficient binom(λ−λ+λ−i,λ−i)=1, giving X(λ−i)Π=E_iλ. For ΠY(λ−j), an input e_k with k<j is carried below e_λ and killed by Π; if k>j the lowering string terminates and gives zero; on e_j its coefficient is binom(λ,λ−j)=binom(λ,j) and its image is e_λ. Therefore ΠY(λ−j)=binom(λ,j)E_λj. All statements include λ=0, when every factor is the identity on the one-dimensional space.

produces.statement: For all i′,j′∈I, Π=E(λ,λ), X(λ−i′)Π=E(i′,λ), and ΠY(λ−j′)=binom(λ,j′)E(λ,j′).

argument.text: Combining F004, or applying it to each e_k, gives X(λ−i)ΠY(λ−j)=binom(λ,j)E_ij. Invert the coefficient using F003 to get E_ij=binom(λ,j)^(-1)X(λ−i)ΠY(λ−j). Every factor on the right preserves M_R by F002 and R-linearity, hence every E_ij preserves M_R. With F002 and F003 this proves the entire exported conclusion.

argument.text: H001 gives λ≥0, so n=λ+1>0 and I consists of exactly n integers. We prove the string identities simultaneously by natural induction on t≥0. At t=0, hv=λv and xv=0 are H003. In the induction step temporarily assume L1: h y^t v=(λ−2t)y^t v and, when t≥1, x y^t v=t(λ−t+1)y^(t−1)v (with xv=0 at t=0). The relation hy=yh−2y from H002 gives h y^(t+1)v=(λ−2t−2)y^(t+1)v. The relation xy=yx+h gives x y^(t+1)v=y(x y^t v)+h y^t v=[t(λ−t+1)+λ−2t]y^t v=(t+1)(λ−t)y^t v, also at t=0 using xv=0. This proves the step and discharges L1; natural induction gives both identities for all t in their stated ranges.

produces.statement: n>0, |I|=n, and for all integers t′≥0, h y^t′ v=(λ−2t′)y^t′ v; for all integers t′≥1, x y^t′ v=t′(λ−t′+1)y^(t′−1)v.

argument.text: For each i∈I, repeated application of the x identity in F001 gives x^i y^i v=i!λ(λ−1)⋯(λ−i+1)v. At i=0 the product is empty and equals 1; at i≥1 its factors are positive integers, since i≤λ. Since v≠0 by H003, this shows e_i≠0 over ℂ. F001 gives h e_i=(λ−2i)e_i. To prove independence, fix coefficients c and temporarily assume L2: Σ_(i∈I)c_i e_i=0. Fix j∈I and apply ∏_(k∈I,k≠j)(h−(λ−2k)Id_V). Every term except j is zero; the j term is c_j [∏_(k≠j)2(k−j)]e_j. All its factors are nonzero complex numbers and e_j≠0, so c_j=0. Since j was arbitrary, all coefficients vanish. Discharging L2 proves independence.

produces.statement: Every e_i′, i′∈I, is nonzero, h e_i′=(λ−2i′)e_i′, and the family e:I→V is complex-linearly independent.

argument.text: Apply M001 to the division ring ℂ, the complex vector space V, the finite index set I and the family e. F002 supplies independence, F001 gives |I|=n, and H002 gives dim_ℂ V=λ+1=n and finite dimensionality. Thus the span of e is V, so together with independence it is a basis. By F001, y^(λ+1)v has eigenvalue −λ−2 under h. Expand this vector in the basis e; comparison of each coefficient in h y^(λ+1)v=(−λ−2)y^(λ+1)v gives [λ−2i−(−λ−2)] times that coefficient zero. For i∈I this multiplier is 2(λ+1−i)≠0 in ℂ. Every coefficient is zero, hence y^(λ+1)v=0. Applying further powers of y gives all higher vanishing.

produces.statement: The family e indexed by I is a complex basis of V, y^(λ+1)v=0, and y^t′ v=0 for all integers t′≥λ+1.

argument.text: For arbitrary i∈I divide the identities F001 by i!: x e_0=0, and for i≥1, x e_i=(λ−i+1)e_(i−1). Directly y e_i=(i+1)e_(i+1) for i<λ, while y e_λ=0 by F003. Also h e_i=(λ−2i)e_i. These are the required integer action matrices.

Fix r≥0. Iterating the x matrix in F004 and dividing by r! gives X(r)e_i=[(λ−i+1)⋯(λ−i+r)/r!]e_(i−r)=binom(λ−i+r,r)e_(i−r) when r≤i. When r>i, iteration reaches x e_0=0 and gives zero. Similarly iteration of y gives Y(r)e_i=[(i+1)⋯(i+r)/r!]e_(i+r)=binom(i+r,r)e_(i+r) if i+r≤λ, and gives zero past the terminating string. These binomial coefficients have nonnegative top at least r. They are integers: for every nonnegative integer a₀, the factorial expressions have boundary values binom(a₀,0)=binom(a₀,a₀)=1 and satisfy binom(a₀,s)=binom(a₀−1,s−1)+binom(a₀−1,s) for 0<s<a₀ by a common-denominator calculation. Induction on a₀, proving the assertion simultaneously for all 0≤s≤a₀, proves integrality. This establishes every divided-power formula in the exported conclusion as well as its zero cases.

argument.text: Use the embedding from N002 throughout to regard M_R as a submodule of V. By N001 its vectors have unique coordinates in e. Since E_ii preserves M_R by N002, the ith coordinate projection maps M_R onto J_i e_i. For arbitrary i,j₁∈I and c₁∈J_(j₁), E(i,j₁)(c₁ e_(j₁))=c₁ e_i∈M_R, giving J_(j₁)⊂J_i; the reverse inclusion follows by exchanging the two coordinate indices. Thus all J_i equal J. Choose the R-basis m of M_R supplied by N002. The finitely many ith coordinates of m generate J_i, since each vector of M_R is a finite R-linear combination of m, and conversely these coordinates lie in J_i by E_ii-stability. Hence J is finitely generated. It is nonzero: temporarily assume L1: J={0}. Then every coordinate projection of M_R would vanish, so M_R would be zero, contradicting its complex span V and the nonzero basis vector e_0 in N001. This contradiction discharges L1 and proves J≠{0}. Finally the maps M_R→J^I taking coordinates, and (c_i)↦Σ c_i e_i, are mutually inverse R-linear maps. The latter sum is in M_R since each c_i e_i is; independence in N001 gives uniqueness. This proves the direct sum decomposition without any rank assumption on a submodule of ℂ.

produces.statement: For every i′∈I, J_i′=J. The R-module J is nonzero and finitely generated. The coordinate map M_R→J^I and its inverse, sending a coefficient family to its finite expansion in e, are R-linear inverses. In particular there is a finite nonempty list of nonzero R-generators of J.

argument.text: Define U and μ as declared, and choose a nonempty finite list g of nonzero R-generators of J from F001; let k≥1 be its length, and write it g_1,...,g_k. For any rational q₀ and any finite R-linear combination Σ_(j=1)^k r_j g_j, tensor bilinearity gives q₀⊗Σ r_j g_j=Σ(q₀r_j)(1⊗g_j). Consequently the finite set {1⊗g_j:1≤j≤k} spans U over ℚ. Apply M008 with F=ℚ and A=U to this finite set; since the span is all of U, U is finite-dimensional. To check injectivity of μ, let s₀≥0 be arbitrary, take arbitrary families Q_1,...,Q_(s₀)∈ℚ and C_1,...,C_(s₀)∈J, and set z₀=Σ_(l=1)^(s₀)Q_l⊗C_l. Every element of the algebraic tensor product has such a finite-sum presentation. Define D to be the product of the positive denominators of the Q_l (the empty product is 1), and put H_l=D Q_l∈ℤ. Then D is a nonzero integer and tensor balancing over R, which contains ℤ, gives z₀=(1/D)⊗Σ H_l C_l. Temporarily assume L2: μ(z₀)=0. Its image is (1/D)Σ H_l C_l, so Σ H_l C_l=0 in ℂ, hence z₀=0 in U. Discharge L2. Since the finite presentation was arbitrary, the kernel of μ is zero, which proves injectivity by applying this to the difference of any two tensors with equal images. Its image is exactly span_ℚ J, since it consists of finite rational combinations of elements of J and contains them all.

produces.statement: U=ℚ⊗_R J is finite-dimensional. The map μ:U→ℂ is injective, satisfies μ(q′⊗c′)=q′·c′ for all q′∈ℚ and c′∈J, and has image span_ℚ J.

argument.text: Define T=ℚ⊗_R M_R. The inclusion R⊂ℚ gives a commutative R-algebra structure on ℚ. Apply M002 to the R-basis m: the n vectors 1⊗m_i form a ℚ-basis of T. M010 applies to the nontrivial commutative ring ℚ. M003 with this basis gives dim_ℚ T=n, since |I|=n by N001.

produces.statement: dim_ℚ T=n, and the vectors 1⊗m_i indexed by I form a ℚ-basis of T.

argument.text: Define Θ:T→U^I by Θ(q₀⊗Σ c_i e_i)=(q₀⊗c_i)_i, and define Ψ in the reverse direction by summing the maps q₀⊗c↦q₀⊗(c e_i) on coordinates. The coordinate maps in F001 are R-linear, so these balanced maps extend to ℚ-linear maps of the indicated tensor products. The composites ΘΨ and ΨΘ are identities: on an elementary tensor in a single coordinate the first is that same coordinate tensor, and on q₀⊗z the second is q₀⊗Σ c_i e_i=q₀⊗z. Additivity and generation by pure tensors prove the identities everywhere. Therefore Θ is a linear equivalence. Set r_J=dim_ℚ U. By F002, U is finitely generated over ℚ, and M009 says it is free. With M010 supplying the strong rank condition for ℚ, apply M004 to the finite constant family U indexed by I; it gives dim_ℚ(U^I)=Σ_(i∈I)r_J=n r_J. Apply M005 to Θ and combine with F003 to obtain n=n r_J. Since n>0 by N001, integer arithmetic yields r_J=1.

produces.statement: dim_ℚ U=r_J=1.

argument.text: Choose a nonzero a∈J from F001. Then 1⊗a is nonzero in U, since μ(1⊗a)=a≠0. The singleton family consisting of 1⊗a is linearly independent: multiplying a putative scalar relation by μ gives that scalar times a zero in ℂ. Apply M001 over ℚ to this singleton and U, whose finite dimension is one by F002 and F004. It spans U. Consequently every 1⊗g_j is q_j(1⊗a) for some rational q_j; apply μ to get g_j=q_j a. As every g_j≠0, each q_j≠0. This proves existence of the full finite rational family needed next.

binders.type: family of nonzero rational numbers indexed by 1,...,k

argument.text: Choose q from F005, and fix 1≤j≤k. Write q_j=A/B with its nonzero integer numerator A and positive integer denominator B. By H001, p≥2, so p≠1. Apply M007 first to |A|≠0, then to B≠0, with ℓ=p. Choose d_N,u_N,d_D,u_D as in those applications, so |A|=p^d_N u_N, B=p^d_D u_D and neither u_N nor u_D is divisible by p. They are nonzero because A,B are. Hence q_j=p^(d_N−d_D)((A/|A|)u_N/u_D). Since A/|A| is either 1 or −1, the rational (A/|A|)u_N/u_D and its inverse belong to R by the defining denominator condition, so this factor is a unit. This proves, for every j in the finite list, the claimed decomposition into an integral power of p and a unit of R, and therefore the existence of simultaneous finite families in F006.

produces.statement: There exist families ν′:{1,...,k}→ℤ and u′:{1,...,k}→Rˣ such that q(j′)=p^(ν′(j′))u′(j′) for every integer j′ with 1≤j′≤k. Here Rˣ means the set of elements of R possessing a multiplicative inverse in R.

argument.text: Choose ν_j,u_j from F006 and let ν be the minimum of the finite nonempty integer list ν_1,...,ν_k; choose j₀ attaining it. Such a minimum exists by repeatedly taking the smaller of two integers. Put b=p^ν a. This is nonzero, since p≠0 and a≠0. For each j, g_j=p^(ν_j−ν)u_j b lies in Rb because ν_j−ν≥0. Conversely g_(j₀)=u_(j₀)b, so b=u_(j₀)^(-1)g_(j₀) belongs to J. Thus the R-module generated by the g_j is exactly Rb, and J=Rb. Under F001, every vector of M_R is a sum Σ r_i b e_i, while any relation Σ r_i b e_i=0 has all r_i b=0 by the complex independence of e in N001, and hence all r_i=0. Thus (b e_i) is an R-basis. The same spanning and independence argument works for any nonzero b with J=Rb. Together with F001, F002 and F004 this proves the exported conclusion.

argument.text: By H001, an integer maps to zero in K exactly when divisible by p. Thus for arbitrary integers A₀,B₀ with B₀≠0 and p∤B₀, the fraction A₀/B₀∈R has a nonzero denominator image in K; and φ(A₀/B₀)=(A₀·1_K)(B₀·1_K)^(-1) is defined. Equality of fractions follows by cross multiplication, so the formula is well-defined and preserves addition, multiplication and 1. The same formula in F_p gives ψ:R→F_p. It is onto, since every integer residue occurs, and its kernel is pR: ψ(A₀/B₀)=0 is equivalent to p∣A₀, hence A₀/B₀=p((A₀/p)/B₀). Conversely multiples of p have zero image. The induced map R/pR→F_p is therefore a bijective ring map. Both constructions agree with the usual inclusion F_p→K. Every unit of R has nonzero image in K, since its image has a multiplicative inverse. In particular N002 shows that r! for 0≤r≤λ and binom(λ,j), j∈I, have nonzero images in K.

produces.statement: φ:R→K and ψ:R→F_p are unital ring maps extending the integer maps, ψ is surjective with kernel pR, R/pR≅F_p, and for 0≤r′≤λ and j′∈I the elements r′! and binom(λ,j′) have nonzero images in K.

argument.text: Define Γ and Γ' by Γ(m⊗c)=(1⊗m)⊗c and Γ'((r⊗m)⊗c)=m⊗φ(r)c. The defining ℤ-balancing relations in R⊗_ℤ M and in M⊗_ℤ K, and the R-balancing relation in M_R⊗_R K, show that these formulas extend to K-linear maps. They are inverse: Γ'Γ(m⊗c)=m⊗c, and ΓΓ'((r⊗m)⊗c)=(1⊗m)⊗φ(r)c=(r⊗m)⊗c. These tensors generate, so the composites are identities. Next define Δ(z⊗c)=[z]⊗c and Δ'([z]⊗c)=z⊗c. Because p acts as zero on K, changing the lift z by pz' changes the second formula by pz'⊗c=z'⊗pc=0. Using F001, scalar balancing in F_p=R/pR gives the remaining balancing condition; thus both maps are well-defined and K-linear. Their composites are identities on pure tensors. This proves the two scalar-extension isomorphisms with exactly the formulas in the exported conclusion. An operator preserving M extends on all these tensors by applying it to the lattice factor; the displayed formulas commute with that operation. For Δ this also holds for any R-linear operator of M_R, since it preserves pM_R.

argument.text: Choose b≠0 with J=Rb from N003. That input proves that (b e_i)_(i∈I), regarded in M_R via the injective map ι_M of N002, is an R-basis. Apply M002 with R₀=R, S₀=K and this basis, using φ from F001. It yields the K-basis (1⊗b e_i) of K⊗_R M_R. The tensor flip z⊗c↦c⊗z is K-linear, well-defined by balancing, and inverse to the reverse flip. Therefore (b e_i⊗1) is a basis of M_R⊗_R K. Transporting it by Γ^(-1) gives the K-basis β_i defined above: inverse linear maps carry spanning families to spanning families and relations to the same relations. Apply M010 to the nontrivial commutative field K, then M003 to β to obtain dim_K V_K=|I|=n>0 using N001.

argument.text: Put a=ρ_K(x⊗1), d=ρ_K(y⊗1), t=ρ_K(h⊗1). By N001, complex linearity gives x(b e_i)=b x e_i, y(b e_i)=b y e_i, and h(b e_i)=b h e_i. The coefficients are the images of the same integers in K. The identical reasoning using N001 for X(r),Y(r) gives their integral divided-power matrices on this basis for all r≥0, including the stated zero cases. Likewise each E_ij preserves M_R by N002 and acts there by E_ij(b e_k)=b e_i if k=j and equals zero otherwise, so its scalar extension, transported by Γ^(-1), is the coordinate matrix unit of β.

argument.text: Fix 0≤r≤λ. As operators on M, the characteristic-zero definitions give r!X(r)=x^r and r!Y(r)=y^r; N002 gives their preservation of M. Tensoring these equalities gives the same equalities of induced operators on V_K. By F001, r!≠0 in K, so the induced divided powers equal (r!)^(-1)a^r and (r!)^(-1)d^r. The equality E_ij=binom(λ,j)^(-1)X(λ−i)Y(λ)X(λ)Y(λ−j) in N002 is an equality of R-linear operators on M_R. Extending scalars and transporting by Γ^(-1) preserves sums and compositions: this follows directly by evaluating on each pure tensor z⊗c. Substitute the divided-power equalities, whose indices λ−i, λ, λ−j all lie between 0 and λ. The result is T_ij=binom(λ,j)^(-1)((λ−i)!)^(-1)a^(λ−i) (λ!)^(-1)d^λ (λ!)^(-1)a^λ ((λ−j)!)^(-1)d^(λ−j), with rightmost factor applied first. Every scalar inverse exists by F001. F004 gives T_ij β_k=β_i if k=j and zero otherwise. 1: # Lean implementation safeguards
2: 
3: Apply these requirements within the accepted NL0 and the fixed Lean interface.
4: They govern implementation, not additional NL0 detail or a weaker Audit B.
5: Use existing library readers and local checking tools; no separate review
6: model, new premise or mandatory lookup of every familiar declaration is needed.
7: 
8: 1. **Check critical library signatures.** Before relying on a critical or
9:    unfamiliar library application, establish its complete type in the pinned
10:    environment, including explicit, implicit and instance binders and all
11:    side conditions. Read the declaration or check a small typed application
12:    when its signature is uncertain. Do not infer the calling convention from
13:    its name or pass an implicit argument as though it were an explicit one.
14:    A previously checked signature in this context need not be looked up again.
15: 2. **Constrain difficult inference.** When coercions or implicit inference
16:    obscure the intended application, give the intermediate fact an explicit
17:    type and supply the relevant named parameters, such as the set, exponent
18:    or ambient space. Prefer this to leaving Lean to discover those choices by
19:    unfolding large definitions. Routine unambiguous arguments can stay
20:    implicit; explicit parameters must preserve the existing target and inputs.
21: 3. **Check conversions before combining them.** When an argument crosses Lean
22:    representations, first establish a small typed conversion fact, then use
23:    it in the main proof. In particular, distinguish `ℝ`, `ℝ≥0` and `ℝ≥0∞`;
24:    check the conversion direction, nonnegativity and any finiteness conditions.
25:    A conversion is not automatically invertible, and matching notation does
26:    not establish equality of differently typed expressions. Reuse a checked
27:    fact when available. Do not invent another representation, a global helper
28:    requirement or an extra hypothesis just to satisfy this instruction.

39: /-- An `sl₂` triple within a Lie ring `L` is a triple of elements `h`, `e`, `f` obeying relations
40: which ensure that the Lie subalgebra they generate is equivalent to `sl₂`. -/
41: structure IsSl2Triple (h e f : L) : Prop where
42:   h_ne_zero : h ≠ 0
43:   lie_e_f : ⁅e, f⁆ = h
44:   lie_h_e_nsmul : ⁅h, e⁆ = 2 • e
45:   lie_h_f_nsmul : ⁅h, f⁆ = -(2 • f)

52: lemma symm (ht : IsSl2Triple h e f) : IsSl2Triple (-h) f e where
53:   h_ne_zero := by simpa using ht.h_ne_zero
54:   lie_e_f := by rw [← neg_eq_iff_eq_neg, lie_skew, ht.lie_e_f]
55:   lie_h_e_nsmul := by rw [neg_lie, neg_eq_iff_eq_neg, ht.lie_h_f_nsmul]

81: theorem matrix_trace_commutator_zero [Fintype n] (X Y : Matrix n n R) : Matrix.trace ⁅X, Y⁆ = 0 :=
82:   calc
83:     _ = Matrix.trace (X * Y) - Matrix.trace (Y * X) := trace_sub _ _
84:     _ = Matrix.trace (X * Y) - Matrix.trace (X * Y) :=
85:       (congr_arg (fun x => _ - x) (Matrix.trace_mul_comm Y X))
86:     _ = 0 := sub_self _

93: /-- The special linear Lie algebra: square matrices of trace zero. -/
94: def sl [Fintype n] : LieSubalgebra R (Matrix n n R) :=
95:   { LinearMap.ker (Matrix.traceLinearMap n R R) with
96:     lie_mem' := fun _ _ => LinearMap.mem_ker.2 <| matrix_trace_commutator_zero _ _ _ _ }
97: 
98: theorem sl_bracket [Fintype n] (A B : sl n R) : ⁅A, B⁆.val = A.val * B.val - B.val * A.val :=

105: /-- When `i ≠ j`, the single-element matrices are elements of `sl n R`.
106: 
107: Along with some elements produced by `singleSubSingle`, these form a natural basis of `sl n R`. -/
108: def single (h : i ≠ j) : R →ₗ[R] sl n R :=
109:   Matrix.singleLinearMap R i j |>.codRestrict _ fun r => Matrix.trace_single_eq_of_ne i j r h

112: theorem val_single (h : i ≠ j) (r : R) : (single i j h r).val = Matrix.single i j r :=
113:   rfl

115: /-- The matrices with matching positive and negative elements on the diagonal are elements of
116: `sl n R`. Along with `single`, a subset of these form a basis for `sl n R`. -/
117: def singleSubSingle : R →ₗ[R] sl n R :=
118:   LinearMap.codRestrict _ (Matrix.singleLinearMap R i i - Matrix.singleLinearMap R j j) fun r =>
119:     LinearMap.sub_mem_ker_iff.mpr <| by simp

12: /-!
13: # Quotienting out a free `ℤ`-module
14: 
15: If `G` is a rank `d` free `ℤ`-module, then `G/nG` is a finite group of cardinality `n ^ d`.
16: -/
17: 
18: @[expose] public section
19: 
20: open Finsupp Function Module
21: 
22: variable {G H M : Type*} [AddCommGroup G] {n : ℕ}
23: 
24: variable (G n) in
25: /-- `ModN G n` denotes the quotient of `G` by multiples of `n` -/
26: abbrev ModN : Type _ := G ⧸ LinearMap.range (LinearMap.lsmul ℤ G n)
27: 
28: namespace ModN
29: 
30: instance : Module (ZMod n) (ModN G n) := QuotientAddGroup.zmodModule (by simp)
31: 
32: set_option backward.isDefEq.respectTransparency false in
33: /-- The universal property of `ModN G n` in terms of monoids: Monoid homomorphisms from `ModN G n`
34: are the same as monoid homomorphisms from `G` whose values are `n`-torsion. -/
35: protected def liftEquiv [AddMonoid M] : (ModN G n →+ M) ≃ {φ : G →+ M // ∀ g, n • φ g = 0} where
36:   toFun f := ⟨f.comp (QuotientAddGroup.mk' _), fun g ↦ by
37:     let Gn : AddSubgroup G := (LinearMap.range (LinearMap.lsmul ℤ G n)).toAddSubgroup
38:     suffices n • g ∈ (QuotientAddGroup.mk' Gn).ker by
39:       simp only [AddMonoidHom.coe_comp, comp_apply, ← map_nsmul]
40:       change f (QuotientAddGroup.mk' Gn (n • g)) = 0 -- Can we avoid `change`?
41:       rw [this, map_zero]
42:     simp [QuotientAddGroup.ker_mk', Gn]⟩
43:   invFun φ := QuotientAddGroup.lift _ φ <| by rintro - ⟨g, rfl⟩; simpa using φ.property g
44:   left_inv f := by
45:     ext x
46:     induction x using QuotientAddGroup.induction_on
47:     rfl -- Should `simp` suffice here?
48:   right_inv φ := by aesop
49: 
50: /-- The universal property of `ModN G n` in terms of `ZMod n`-modules: `ZMod n`-linear maps from
51: `ModN G n` are the same as monoid homomorphisms from `G` whose values are `n`-torsion. -/
52: protected def liftEquiv' [AddCommGroup H] [Module (ZMod n) H] :
53:     (ModN G n →ₗ[ZMod n] H) ≃ {φ : G →+ H // ∀ g, n • φ g = 0} :=
54:   (AddMonoidHom.toZModLinearMapEquiv n).symm.toEquiv.trans ModN.liftEquiv
55: 
56: variable (n) in
57: /-- The quotient map `G → G / nG`. -/
58: def mkQ : G →+ ModN G n := (LinearMap.range (LinearMap.lsmul ℤ G n)).mkQ
59: 
60: variable [NeZero n]
61: 
62: set_option backward.isDefEq.respectTransparency false in
63: /-- Given a free module `G` over `ℤ`, construct the corresponding basis
64: of `G / ⟨n⟩` over `ℤ / nℤ`. -/
65: noncomputable def basis {ι : Type*} (b : Basis ι ℤ G) : Basis ι (ZMod n) (ModN G n) := by
66:   set ψ : G →+ G := zsmulAddGroupHom n
67:   set nG := LinearMap.range (LinearMap.lsmul ℤ G n)
68:   set H := G ⧸ nG
69:   set φ : G →ₗ[ℤ] H := nG.mkQ
70:   let mod : (ι →₀ ℤ) →ₗ[ℤ] (ι →₀ ZMod n) := mapRange.linearMap (Int.castAddHom _).toIntLinearMap
71:   let f : G →ₗ[ℤ] (ι →₀ ℤ) := b.repr
72:   have hker : nG ≤ LinearMap.ker (mod.comp f) := by
73:     rintro _ ⟨x, rfl⟩
74:     ext b
75:     simp [mod, f]
76:   let g : H →ₗ[ℤ] (ι →₀ ZMod n) := nG.liftQ (mod.comp f) hker
77:   refine ⟨.ofBijective (g.toAddMonoidHom.toZModLinearMap n) ⟨?_, ?_⟩⟩
78:   · rw [AddMonoidHom.coe_toZModLinearMap, LinearMap.toAddMonoidHom_coe, injective_iff_map_eq_zero,
79:       nG.mkQ_surjective.forall]
80:     intro x hx
81:     simp only [Submodule.mkQ_apply, g] at hx
82:     rw [Submodule.liftQ_apply] at hx
83:     replace hx : ∀ b, ↑n ∣ f x b := by
84:       simpa [mod, DFunLike.ext_iff, ZMod.intCast_zmod_eq_zero_iff_dvd] using! hx
85:     simp only [Submodule.mkQ_apply]
86:     rw [Submodule.Quotient.mk_eq_zero]
87:     choose c hc using hx
88:     refine ⟨b.repr.symm ⟨(f x).support, c, by simp [hc, NeZero.ne]⟩, b.repr.injective ?_⟩
89:     simpa [DFunLike.ext_iff, eq_comm] using! hc
90:   · suffices mod ∘ b.repr = g ∘ nG.mkQ by
91:       exact (this ▸ (mapRange_surjective _ (map_zero _) ZMod.intCast_surjective).comp
92:         b.repr.surjective).of_comp
93:     ext x b
94:     simp [mod, g, f, H]
95: 
96: set_option backward.isDefEq.respectTransparency false in
97: lemma basis_apply_eq_mkQ {ι : Type*} (b : Basis ι ℤ G) (i : ι) : basis b i = mkQ n (b i) := by
98:   rw [Basis.apply_eq_iff]; simp [basis, mkQ]
99: 
100: variable [Module.Free ℤ G] [Module.Finite ℤ G]
101: 
102: instance instModuleFinite : Module.Finite (ZMod n) (ModN G n) :=
103:   .of_basis <| basis <| Module.Free.chooseBasis ℤ G
104: 
105: instance instFinite : Finite (ModN G n) := Module.finite_of_finite (ZMod n)
106: 
107: variable (G n)
108: @[simp] lemma natCard_eq : Nat.card (ModN G n) = n ^ Module.finrank ℤ G := by
109:   simp [Nat.card_congr (basis <| Module.Free.chooseBasis ℤ G).repr.toEquiv,
110:     Nat.card_eq_fintype_card, Module.finrank_eq_card_chooseBasisIndex]
111: 
112: end ModN

314: /-- When `f` is an `R`-linear map taking values in `S`, then `fun b ↦ f b • x` is an `R`-linear
315: map. -/
316: def smulRight (f : M₁ →ₗ[R] S) (x : M) : M₁ →ₗ[R] M where
317:   toFun b := f b • x
318:   map_add' x y := by rw [f.map_add, add_smul]
319:   map_smul' b y := by rw [RingHom.id_apply, map_smul, smul_assoc]
320: 
321: @[simp]
322: theorem coe_smulRight (f : M₁ →ₗ[R] S) (x : M) : (smulRight f x : M₁ → M) = fun c => f c • x :=
323:   rfl
324: 
325: theorem smulRight_apply (f : M₁ →ₗ[R] S) (x : M) (c : M₁) : smulRight f x c = f c • x :=
326:   rfl
327: 
328: @[simp]
329: lemma smulRight_zero (f : M₁ →ₗ[R] S) : f.smulRight (0 : M) = 0 := by ext; simp

653: 
654: end Equiv
655: 
656: section Coord
657: 
658: variable (i : ι)
659: 
660: /-- `b.coord i` is the linear function giving the `i`-th coordinate of a vector
661: with respect to the basis `b`.
662: 
663: `b.coord i` is an element of the dual space. In particular, for
664: finite-dimensional spaces it is the `ι`th basis vector of the dual space.
665: -/
666: @[simps!]
667: def coord : M →ₗ[R] R :=
668:   Finsupp.lapply i ∘ₗ ↑b.repr
669: 
670: theorem forall_coord_eq_zero_iff {x : M} : (∀ i, b.coord i x = 0) ↔ x = 0 :=
671:   Iff.trans (by simp only [b.coord_apply, DFunLike.ext_iff, Finsupp.zero_apply])
672:     b.repr.map_eq_zero_iff
673: 
674: /-- The sum of the coordinates of an element `m : M` with respect to a basis. -/
675: noncomputable def sumCoords : M →ₗ[R] R :=
676:   (Finsupp.lsum ℕ fun _ => LinearMap.id) ∘ₗ (b.repr : M →ₗ[R] ι →₀ R)
677: 
678: @[simp]
679: theorem coe_sumCoords : (b.sumCoords : M → R) = fun m => (b.repr m).sum fun _ => id :=
680:   rfl
681: 
682: @[simp high]
683: theorem coe_sumCoords_of_fintype [Fintype ι] : (b.sumCoords : M → R) = ∑ i, b.coord i := by
684:   ext m
